# A finding that contradicts what everyone knows. {.unnumbered background-color="#003594"}

## Firearm death is understood as an urban problem, and Pennsylvania's data disagrees

Firearm injury is commonly described as a problem of cities. Pennsylvania's county-level
data, correctly assembled, reports a **higher** firearm death rate outside metropolitan
counties than inside them.

::: {.callout-important}
## The question this session opens
Which Pennsylvania counties carry the highest burden of firearm death — and does the answer
depend on how the analysis handles the counties that report nothing?

**This session establishes the pipeline as a single reproducible object**: import, clean,
join, group, summarise, visualise, report — one document another person can run.
:::

**Required from Modules 4 and 5:** `pd.read_csv()`, `.dropna()`, `.merge()`, `.groupby()`,
`.agg()`, and `plt.subplots()`.

::: {.notes}
Ask the room first, before any code is on screen. Where in Pennsylvania would you expect the
firearm death rate to be highest? Take three answers. Somebody says Philadelphia, somebody
says Pittsburgh, and that is the honest expectation — it is what the news covers and it is
not a stupid answer.

Then tell them the data disagrees, and do not tell them by how much yet. Today they build
the analysis that shows it.

Here is what makes this session different from every other one. In five modules the finding
confirmed what a public-health student already suspected. Poverty tracks infant mortality.
Smoking tracks asthma. Those were real, and they were reassuring. This one is not reassuring,
and it is the only finding in the course designed to surprise them.

And the reason it surprises is the part worth teaching. It is not that everyone was wrong
about cities. It is that the obvious way to compute this number gives the opposite answer,
and the obvious way is wrong for a reason they can see and fix. That is the whole session.

One thing to say out loud early, because it sets the frame for the next seventy-five minutes.
This is injury prevention. Roughly six in ten of these deaths are suicides, which is a mental
health and means-access story, not a crime story. This course treats it that way, and the
writeup they turn in should too.
:::

## This session is one working session, and the project starts in it

| | |
|---|---|
| **First twenty minutes** | The pipeline as one object, and the one error that reverses this finding |
| **The rest of the session** | Studio — build the analysis, end to end, on the real data |
| **What leaves the room** | A document that runs top to bottom, and the paragraph that reports it |

::: {.callout-note}
## The writeup is thirty percent of the final grade
The final project is assessed on the analysis and on the report of it. A correct pipeline
described badly loses more points than a modest pipeline described precisely.
:::

::: {.notes}
Say the structure plainly so nobody is waiting for a lab on Thursday. There is no Thursday.
This is the combined session, the calendar says so, and what they build today is the skeleton
of the project they present on December 1st and 3rd.

Be blunt about the thirty percent. Every semester a few students treat the writing as
something to do at 2am after the code works. The rubric does not agree. A student who gets
nonmetro 18.5 and writes one careful paragraph about what it means and what it does not
outscores a student with a beautiful notebook and no argument.

The studio time is real work time. Circulate. The exercises are built so that the sixth one
is the one that breaks people, and that is deliberate.
:::

## The pipeline is seven stages, and the whole session is one pass through it {.smaller}

| Stage | Verb | Module |
|---|---|---|
| **Import** | `pd.read_csv()` | 4 |
| **Clean** | `.dropna()`, `.fillna()`, `.astype()` | 4 |
| **Join** | `.merge()` | 4 |
| **Group** | `.groupby()` | 4 |
| **Summarise** | `.agg()`, derived columns | 4 |
| **Visualise** | `plt.subplots()`, `ax.bar()` | 5 |
| **Report** | prose, with the numbers in it | 6 |

Every stage has already been taught. **The new skill is running all seven as one object that
another person can execute and get the same answer.**

::: {.notes}
Point at the right-hand column, because it is the reassuring part. There is exactly one new
row in this table, and it is the last one. Everything above it they already did in the last
two modules.

What is new is the seam between the stages. Individually they can each merge and each group.
The thing they have never done is hold all seven in one document in an order that survives
being run by somebody else, on a different machine, three weeks later. That is a genuinely
different skill and it is the one employers actually notice.

The word to keep saying today is *pipeline*, singular. Not "my analysis code." One object,
with an input at one end and a claim at the other.
:::

## The data is two files, and the join is the reason there are two {.smaller}

```{pyodide}
import pandas as pd

firearm = pd.read_csv("data/pa_firearm_county_year.csv")
counties = pd.read_csv("data/pa_counties.csv")

print(firearm.shape, counties.shape)
print(firearm.columns.tolist())
print(counties.columns.tolist())
```

`pa_firearm_county_year.csv` has 402 rows — 67 counties × 6 years, 2019–2024. It carries
deaths and it does not carry **metro status**. `pa_counties.csv` carries metro status and it
does not carry deaths.

::: {.callout-note}
## Source
CDC, *Mapping Injury, Overdose, and Violence — County* (`psx4-wq38`); Census CO-EST2023 and
the NCHS Urban–Rural Classification, 2013.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the honest motivation for the join, and it is the same one from Module 4. The
question is about metro against nonmetro. The word "metro" appears in exactly one of these
two files, and the deaths appear in the other. There is no way to answer the question without
putting them together, which is why merge is not a party trick.

Worth naming the classification, since a student will ask what counts as metro. It is the
NCHS urban–rural scheme, six levels collapsed to two, and it is assigned by the federal
government rather than by the instructor. Thirty-seven metro counties, thirty nonmetro.
:::

## Forty percent of the cells report no number, and the reason is protective {.smaller}

```{pyodide}
print(firearm["firearm_deaths"].isna().sum(), "of", len(firearm), "rows suppressed")
print(firearm[firearm["year"] == 2023]["firearm_deaths"].isna().sum(), "of 67 in 2023")
```

CDC suppresses a county-year cell when the count is small enough that publishing it could
identify a decedent. **159 of 402 cells** carry no number. In 2023, **25 of 67 counties**
report nothing.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Suppression is not random, and that is the whole problem
Cells are suppressed **because the count is small**. Small counts occur in **small counties**,
and small counties are **disproportionately nonmetro** — 19 of 30 nonmetro counties are
suppressed in 2023, against 6 of 37 metro counties.
:::

::: {.notes}
Take a moment on why suppression exists, because students arrive assuming missing data is
sloppiness. It is the opposite of sloppiness. If a county of four thousand people had one
firearm death last year and the agency published it, somebody reading the local paper could
work out who. The blank is a deliberate act of protection, and the right response to it is
not irritation.

Now the sentence that matters for today. Missingness here is not a coin flip. It is caused by
the very thing being measured — small counts — and small counts live in small rural counties.
Nineteen of thirty nonmetro counties versus six of thirty-seven metro. That is a structural
pattern, not noise.

Hold that thought for two slides, because it is about to eat the analysis alive.
:::

## The pooled rate is total deaths over total population {.smaller}

```{pyodide}
demo_2023 = firearm[firearm["year"] == 2023]
demo_reporting = demo_2023.dropna(subset=["firearm_deaths"])

demo_joined = demo_reporting.merge(
    counties[["county", "metro", "region", "population_2023"]],
    on="county", how="left"
)

demo_summary = demo_joined.groupby("metro").agg(
    counties=("county", "size"),
    deaths=("firearm_deaths", "sum"),
    population=("population_2023", "sum"),
)
demo_summary["rate_per_100k"] = demo_summary["deaths"] / demo_summary["population"] * 100000
print(demo_summary.round(1))
```

A pooled rate sums the numerators and sums the denominators, then divides once. It is not the
average of the county rates.

::: {.notes}
Walk the four lines slowly, because this is the shape of every pipeline they will ever write.
Filter to a year. Drop the rows with no number. Join on the grouping variable. Group and
aggregate. Four verbs, all from Module 4.

The one line to defend is the dropna, and it is on the next slide, so resist explaining it
here. Let them see the output first.

The distinction at the bottom is worth thirty seconds. Pooling is not averaging. If the
sixty-seven county rates are averaged with equal weight, Cameron County with four thousand
people counts as much as Philadelphia with a million and a half. Pooling weights by
population, which is what a state-level rate means. Both are legitimate and they answer
different questions; today is pooled.
:::

## The same analysis without the `.dropna()` reverses the finding {.smaller}

```{pyodide}
demo_naive = demo_2023.merge(counties[["county", "metro", "population_2023"]],
                             on="county", how="left")
demo_wrong = demo_naive.groupby("metro").agg(
    deaths=("firearm_deaths", "sum"),
    population=("population_2023", "sum"),
)
demo_wrong["rate_per_100k"] = demo_wrong["deaths"] / demo_wrong["population"] * 100000
print(demo_wrong.round(1))
```

| 2023, pooled | Correct | Without `.dropna()` |
|---|---|---|
| Metro | **14.1** | 13.6 |
| Nonmetro | **18.5** | **8.2** |

`.sum()` skips missing values, and the population column does not. A suppressed county
therefore contributes **its full population to the denominator and zero deaths to the
numerator**, which drags the group rate downward — hardest where suppression concentrates.

::: {.callout-important}
## This error raises no exception
Both versions run. Both produce a clean table. One says nonmetro rates are lower.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the most important slide in the module. Slow all the way down.

Ask them to read the second column out loud. Eight point two against thirteen point six.
Nonmetro looks *safer*, by a lot, and it confirms exactly what the room guessed twenty minutes
ago. If a student handed that table in, it would look completely reasonable. The code is
clean. Nothing errored. The numbers have the right number of decimal places.

And it is wrong, for a reason that fits in one sentence: sum skips NaN and the denominator
does not. Nineteen nonmetro counties put their entire population into the bottom of that
fraction and contributed no deaths to the top, because their deaths were suppressed for
privacy. The rate is not measuring firearm death. It is measuring how much nonmetro
population got parked in a denominator with nothing above it.

The fix is one line and they have known it since Module 4. Drop the rows with no number
*before* the join, so a county that reports nothing is out of both halves of the fraction.

Then the sentence that is really about the rest of their careers. This error is silent. There
is no exception, no warning, no red text. In Module 5 the lesson was that a figure can run
and lie. Today it is that a table can run and lie, and the only defence is knowing what your
denominator contains. Say it exactly like that.
:::

## The suicide share explains the gap {.smaller}

```{pyodide}
demo_joined["suicides"] = demo_joined["firearm_suicide"].fillna(0)

demo_share = demo_joined.groupby("metro").agg(
    deaths=("firearm_deaths", "sum"),
    suicides=("suicides", "sum"),
)
demo_share["suicide_share_pct"] = demo_share["suicides"] / demo_share["deaths"] * 100
print(demo_share.round(1))
```

Among counties reporting a death count, **62.1%** of nonmetro firearm deaths are suicides,
against **54.7%** in metro counties.

::: {.callout-note}
## The definition is part of the finding
Suppressed suicide counts are treated as zero here, across the counties that report a death
total. Restricting instead to counties reporting **both** columns gives 83.7% for nonmetro —
a different, much smaller denominator. **The number moves when the definition moves, so the
definition is stated with the number.**
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the answer to the "but why" that the previous slide raises. A higher nonmetro rate is
a finding. It is not yet an explanation, and a finding without a mechanism is where a lot of
student writeups stop.

Sixty-two percent against fifty-five. The nonmetro burden is more heavily suicide, and that
is consistent with everything known about firearm injury in rural America — higher household
firearm ownership, greater physical isolation, thinner mental health infrastructure, and
longer distances to emergency care. Suicide attempts with a firearm are lethal in roughly
eighty-five percent of cases, against a few percent for most other means, so access to a
firearm converts a crisis into a death at a rate nothing else matches.

Now the callout, which is a methods lesson wearing a public health hat. There are two
defensible ways to compute that share and they differ by twenty-two points. Not because
anyone cheated — because the suicide column is suppressed more often than the death column,
so restricting to rows with both quietly throws away counties. Whichever one is chosen, it
gets stated in the writeup. An unlabelled 62% is not a number, it is a rumour.
:::

## The finding holds across six years, so it is not one unusual year {.smaller}

```{pyodide}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

allyears = firearm.dropna(subset=["firearm_deaths"]).merge(
    counties[["county", "metro"]], on="county", how="left"
)
trend = (allyears.groupby(["year", "metro"])
         .apply(lambda g: g["firearm_deaths"].sum() / g["population"].sum() * 100000)
         .unstack())

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.4))
ax.plot(trend.index, trend["Nonmetro"], marker="^", linewidth=2.5,
        color="#8a6400", label="Nonmetro")
ax.plot(trend.index, trend["Metro"], marker="o", linewidth=2.5,
        color="#003594", label="Metro")
ax.set_xlabel("Year")
ax.set_ylabel("Firearm deaths per 100,000")
ax.set_title("Pooled firearm death rate, reporting PA counties, 2019–2024")
ax.set_ylim(0, 22)
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print(trend.round(1))
```

::: {.figure-description}
**Figure 1.** Line chart of pooled firearm death rate per 100,000 for reporting Pennsylvania
counties, 2019 to 2024, with two series distinguished by both colour and marker shape.
Nonmetro counties, drawn in dark gold with triangular markers, run at 18.0 in 2019, dip to
13.4 in 2020, then rise to 16.3, 16.1, and 18.5 before falling to 15.7 in 2024. Metro
counties, drawn in royal blue with circular markers, rise from 11.6 in 2019 to a peak of 15.3
in 2022, then fall to 14.1 and 12.4. The nonmetro line sits above the metro line in five of
the six years; the exception is 2020.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the reproducibility argument made visually. One year could be a fluke, and a careful
reader is entitled to ask whether 2023 was cherry-picked. Five of six years say the same
thing, and the exception is 2020, which is the pandemic year that behaves strangely in every
dataset in this course.

Point at the marker shapes deliberately. Triangles and circles, not just gold and blue. From
Module 5: those two colours are each perfectly legible against white and they do not reliably
separate from *each other* — two point oh two to one. Colour is never the only channel, and
that rule does not relax because the figure is going in a report.

The zero baseline matters here too. Setting the y-limit to start at zero rather than at
thirteen is what keeps a four-point gap looking like a four-point gap.

Mention the counties-reporting-per-year caveat if anyone is sharp enough to ask: the nonmetro
line is built from seven to eleven counties depending on the year, so it moves more than the
metro line. That is real instability, and it is the honest thing to put in the writeup rather
than hide.
:::

## Notebook hygiene is what makes the result reproducible {.smaller}

| Rule | Reason |
|---|---|
| **Imports in the first cell** | A notebook that only runs after scrolling up is broken |
| **Restart and run all, before submitting** | Out-of-order state is invisible until it is fatal |
| **Relative paths** — `data/file.csv` | `/Users/soumik/Desktop/...` runs on exactly one machine |
| **`np.random.seed(...)`** if anything is random | Same input, same output, every time |
| **No manual edits to output** | A number typed by hand is not a result |

::: {.callout-warning}
## The failure this prevents
A notebook where cell 12 was run, then cell 4 was edited, holds a value in memory that no
longer matches any code on screen. **The document is the record, not the memory.**
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the section that sounds like housekeeping and is actually the difference between an
analysis and a rumour.

Tell them the restart-and-run-all story, because everyone has a version of it. A student
builds something over four hours, it works, they close the laptop. They reopen it the next
morning and nothing runs, because half the variables they depended on were defined in cells
they later deleted or edited. The notebook never told them, because the values were sitting in
memory the whole time. Kernel restart, run all, from the top — before submitting anything.
Every time. It takes thirty seconds and it is the single highest-value habit in this course.

The absolute-path one is worth a live demonstration if there is time. A path starting with
slash Users slash somebody's name runs on precisely one computer on Earth. Their project gets
opened by a grader on a different machine, and a data-slash-filename path just works.

The last row is the ethics row, so do not skip it. If the code prints 18.4 and the writeup
says 18.5 because that looked tidier, that is fabrication. Small, harmless-feeling, and
still fabrication. The number in the prose comes from the cell above it.
:::

## Uncertainty is reported in words, with the counts that produced it {.smaller}

The nonmetro rate is built from **11 counties and 116 deaths**. The metro rate is built from
**31 counties and 1,567 deaths**. A rate computed from a small number of events moves a great
deal when one event is added or removed.

| Written honestly | Written badly |
|---|---|
| "18.5 per 100,000, from 116 deaths across 11 reporting counties" | "18.5 per 100,000" |
| "Suppression removes 19 of 30 nonmetro counties" | "Nonmetro counties: 18.5" |
| "The gap holds in five of six years" | "Nonmetro rates are higher" |

::: {.callout-note}
## This course does not compute p-values
Uncertainty is described: how many events, how many counties, how much the estimate moves
between years, and what suppression removed. **A p-value is not required to report an
estimate honestly, and it is not a substitute for reporting the counts.**
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the §8 slide and it is the one an outside reviewer would flag, so say the reasoning
out loud rather than hiding it.

They have not had inference. No t-tests, no confidence intervals, no p-values. That is a
deliberate choice about what fits in six weeks, and here is the defence: a p-value they cannot
interpret is worth less than a count they can. Telling a reader the estimate rests on 116
deaths in 11 counties conveys the fragility directly, in a form nobody misreads. A star next
to a number does not.

Juniata County is the concrete example and it is a good one. Ten deaths, twenty-three thousand
people, forty-three per hundred thousand — the highest county rate in the state that year. Ask
the room what happens to that number if two of those ten deaths had happened in December of
the previous year. It drops to thirty-four. Same county, same reality, different bin. That is
what an unstable rate means, and no student needs a distributional assumption to feel it.

For their projects the rule is simple: never report a rate without the count it came from.
:::

## The report is the deliverable, and it has a fixed shape {.smaller}

| Move | One or two sentences |
|---|---|
| **The question** | What was asked, of which population, in which years |
| **The data** | Source, coverage, and **what is missing and why** |
| **The method** | The pipeline in prose — filtered, dropped, joined, pooled |
| **The finding** | The numbers, with their denominators |
| **The limit** | What this design cannot establish |

::: {.callout-important}
## Integrating computer output
Output is **evidence inside a sentence**, never a pasted block left to speak for itself.
✗ A bare table dropped into the document.
✓ "Among the 42 counties reporting a 2023 count, the pooled nonmetro rate was 18.5 per
100,000 against 14.1 in metro counties (Table 1)."
:::

::: {.notes}
Give them the shape explicitly, because "write it up" is useless advice and this table is not.
Five moves. A paragraph each, or less. That is a report.

The move students skip is the last one, and it is the one that separates a public-health
writeup from a blog post. What this design cannot establish: these are county aggregates, so
a pattern across counties describes counties and not the individuals in them — that is the
ecological fallacy, and it applies here exactly as it did to smoking and asthma last week.
Metro status is not a cause of anything. It is a label that travels with firearm ownership,
isolation, and access to care.

On the callout: the commonest failure in the drafts is a screenshot of a DataFrame sitting
alone in the middle of a page, doing no work. A table is an exhibit. A sentence points at the
exhibit and says what to see in it. Show them the good version and read it aloud — it names
the coverage, gives both numbers, and cites the table, in one breath.

One more, and be firm because it comes up every year: generative AI is not permitted in this
course. The writeup is assessed as their reasoning about their own analysis.
:::

## The finding, stated as it would appear in a report {.smaller}

> Among the 42 Pennsylvania counties reporting a 2023 firearm death count, the pooled death
> rate was **18.5 per 100,000 in nonmetropolitan counties** and **14.1 per 100,000 in
> metropolitan counties**. Suicides account for **62.1%** of nonmetropolitan firearm deaths
> and **54.7%** of metropolitan ones. Because CDC suppresses small counts, 25 of 67 counties
> report no 2023 total, and suppression is concentrated in nonmetropolitan counties (19 of
> 30). Counties reporting no total are excluded from both the numerator and the denominator;
> retaining their population while summing only reported deaths reverses the comparison to
> 8.2 against 13.6. The nonmetropolitan rate exceeds the metropolitan rate in five of the six
> years from 2019 to 2024.

::: {.callout-note}
## What this paragraph does
It states the numbers, the coverage, the definition, the sensitivity, and the consistency
check. It makes no causal claim.
:::

::: {.notes}
Read this paragraph out loud, slowly, and then say: that is the whole assignment. Not the
notebook — this. Six sentences, every one carrying a number, no adjectives doing any work.

Have them count what is in it. The estimate. The denominator. The definitional choice. The
sensitivity analysis, which is the sentence about 8.2 and 13.6 — that is the alternative
specification, named and reported rather than buried. And the robustness, which is five of six
years. That is a professional paragraph, and no student in the room could not have written it
by the end of today.

Then point at what is *not* in it. No "shockingly." No "this proves." No mechanism asserted
without evidence. The suicide share is offered as consistent with an explanation, and the
paragraph stops there, because that is where the data stops.

This is the target for the studio. Their project paragraph will have a different question in
it, and the same five moves.
:::

## Studio {.smaller}

The remainder of the session is build time. **Nine exercises assemble the pipeline in the
order it runs**, and the last one produces the paragraph.

| | |
|---|---|
| **1–3** | Import, inspect, and clean — including the suppression decision |
| **4–5** | Join, then group and summarise |
| **6** | The silent error, reproduced deliberately and repaired |
| **7–8** | Visualise, with a description and a zero baseline |
| **9** | Write the finding |

::: {.callout-tip}
## This is the project skeleton
The final project replaces the question and the dataset. **The seven stages do not change.**
:::

::: {.notes}
Set them going and then circulate rather than lecturing over the top of it.

Exercise 6 is the one to watch for. It hands them the wrong pipeline, running cleanly, and
asks what is wrong with it — and a good number of students will stare at correct-looking code
for several minutes before the denominator occurs to them. That struggle is the point, so do
not rescue anyone too early. Ask them what is in the bottom of the fraction and walk away.

For anyone who finishes early, the extension is in the final callout: run the same pipeline
grouped by region instead of metro status, six groups instead of two, and see whether the
story survives a finer cut. It mostly does, and the counties get thin enough that the
instability lesson lands a second time on its own.

Remind them at about the twenty-minute mark to restart and run all. Some of them will already
have out-of-order state, and finding that now is much cheaper than finding it in December.
:::

# Exercise 1 — Import and inspect {.unnumbered background-color="#003594"}

## Exercise 1 — Import and inspect

**Worked example.** A pipeline opens by loading its inputs and confirming their shape. An
analysis that never checks what arrived is an analysis that trusts a file it has not read.

```{pyodide}
import pandas as pd

firearm = pd.read_csv("data/pa_firearm_county_year.csv")

print(firearm.shape)
print(firearm["year"].min(), "to", firearm["year"].max())
print(firearm["firearm_deaths"].isna().sum(), "suppressed cells")
```

# Exercise 3 — Clean, and decide about the blanks {.unnumbered background-color="#003594"}

## Exercise 3 — Clean, and decide about the blanks

**Worked example.** `.dropna(subset=[...])` removes rows missing a value in the named column
and leaves every other column alone. Naming the column matters: dropping on the whole frame
would also discard counties whose *homicide* count is suppressed but whose total is known.

```{pyodide}
careless = f2023.dropna()
print("dropna() on everything:", len(careless), "counties left")
```

# Exercise 4 — Join {.unnumbered background-color="#003594"}

## Exercise 4 — Join

**Worked example.** `.merge()` attaches columns from a second table by matching on a shared
key. `how="left"` keeps every row of the left table whether or not it finds a match, which
makes an unmatched key visible instead of silent.

```{pyodide}
example = reporting.merge(county_reference[["county", "region"]], on="county", how="left")
print(example[["county", "firearm_deaths", "region"]].head(3))
print(example["region"].isna().sum(), "rows failed to match")
```

## Exercise 4 — Join — your turn

**Your turn.** Merge `reporting` with the `county`, `metro`, and `population_2023` columns of
`counties`, matching **on county**. Confirm nothing failed to match.

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex4_join
joined = reporting.merge(
    county_reference[["county", "metro", "population_2023"]],
    ______="county",
    how="left"
)

print(joined.shape)
print(joined["metro"].isna().sum(), "rows failed to match")
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex4_join
#| hint: true
# The blank is on.
#
# `on="county"` says the two tables are lined up by county name. If these
# files spelled a county differently — the real "Mc Kean" / "McKean" bug
# from Module 4 — that county would arrive with a missing metro value,
# which is exactly what the second print statement is checking for.
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex4_join
#| solution: true
joined = reporting.merge(
    county_reference[["county", "metro", "population_2023"]],
    on="county",
    how="left"
)

print(joined.shape)
print(joined["metro"].isna().sum(), "rows failed to match")
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex4_join
#| check: true
assert len(joined) == 42, "The join must not change the row count: 42."
assert "metro" in joined.columns, "The metro column must arrive from counties."
assert joined["metro"].isna().sum() == 0, "Every county must match. None should be missing."
assert joined["population_2023"].sum() == 11748170, "Populations should total 11,748,170."
```

# Exercise 5 — Group and summarise {.unnumbered background-color="#003594"}

## Exercise 5 — Group and summarise

**Worked example.** `.groupby().agg()` collapses many rows into one row per group, naming
each output column and the operation that fills it. `"size"` counts rows; `"sum"` totals a
column.

```{pyodide}
by_region = (reporting
             .merge(county_reference[["county", "region"]], on="county", how="left")
             .groupby("region")
             .agg(counties=("county", "size"),
                  deaths=("firearm_deaths", "sum")))
print(by_region)
```

## Exercise 5 — Group and summarise — your turn

**Your turn.** Group `joined` by `metro`. Total the deaths and the population, then add a
`rate_per_100k` column.

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex5_group
summary = joined.groupby("metro").agg(
    counties=("county", "size"),
    deaths=("firearm_deaths", "sum"),
    population=("population_2023", "sum"),
)

summary["rate_per_100k"] = summary["deaths"] / summary["______"] * 100000
print(summary.round(1))
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex5_group
#| hint: true
# The blank is population — the column you just created inside .agg().
#
# A rate is events divided by the population at risk, scaled. Multiplying
# by 100,000 is what makes it "per 100,000" rather than a proportion.
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex5_group
#| solution: true
summary = joined.groupby("metro").agg(
    counties=("county", "size"),
    deaths=("firearm_deaths", "sum"),
    population=("population_2023", "sum"),
)

summary["rate_per_100k"] = summary["deaths"] / summary["population"] * 100000
print(summary.round(1))
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex5_group
#| check: true
assert "rate_per_100k" in summary.columns, "Add a rate_per_100k column."
assert round(summary.loc["Nonmetro", "rate_per_100k"], 1) == 18.5, "Nonmetro should be 18.5."
assert round(summary.loc["Metro", "rate_per_100k"], 1) == 14.1, "Metro should be 14.1."
assert summary.loc["Nonmetro", "counties"] == 11, "11 nonmetro counties report."
```

::: {.callout-important}
## That is the finding
**18.5 against 14.1.** The rate outside metropolitan Pennsylvania is higher, and it was
produced by five ordinary lines of pandas.
:::

# Exercise 6 — The error that raises nothing {.unnumbered background-color="#003594"}

## Exercise 6 — The error that raises nothing

**Worked example.** The pipeline below is identical to Exercise 5 except for one omission. It
runs without complaint and returns the opposite finding.

```{pyodide}
broken = f2023.merge(county_reference[["county", "metro", "population_2023"]],
                     on="county", how="left")
broken_summary = broken.groupby("metro").agg(
    deaths=("firearm_deaths", "sum"),
    population=("population_2023", "sum"),
)
broken_summary["rate_per_100k"] = (broken_summary["deaths"]
                                   / broken_summary["population"] * 100000)
print(broken_summary.round(1))
```

The suppressed counties were never removed. `.sum()` skips their missing deaths; the
population column does not skip their people.

## Exercise 6 — The error that raises nothing — your turn

**Your turn.** Repair it. Drop the non-reporting counties **before** the merge, and confirm
the nonmetro rate returns to 18.5.

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex6_silent
repaired = f2023.______(subset=["firearm_deaths"]).merge(
    county_reference[["county", "metro", "population_2023"]], on="county", how="left"
)

fixed = repaired.groupby("metro").agg(
    deaths=("firearm_deaths", "sum"),
    population=("population_2023", "sum"),
)
fixed["rate_per_100k"] = fixed["deaths"] / fixed["population"] * 100000

print(fixed.round(1))
print("population dropped from the denominator:",
      broken_summary["population"].sum() - fixed["population"].sum())
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex6_silent
#| hint: true
# The blank is dropna.
#
# Think about what belongs in a denominator. A rate's denominator is the
# population a counted event could have happened to. If a county's deaths
# were never published, its people cannot be in the bottom of the fraction
# while nothing of theirs is in the top.
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex6_silent
#| solution: true
repaired = f2023.dropna(subset=["firearm_deaths"]).merge(
    county_reference[["county", "metro", "population_2023"]], on="county", how="left"
)

fixed = repaired.groupby("metro").agg(
    deaths=("firearm_deaths", "sum"),
    population=("population_2023", "sum"),
)
fixed["rate_per_100k"] = fixed["deaths"] / fixed["population"] * 100000

print(fixed.round(1))
print("population dropped from the denominator:",
      broken_summary["population"].sum() - fixed["population"].sum())
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex6_silent
#| check: true
assert round(fixed.loc["Nonmetro", "rate_per_100k"], 1) == 18.5, "Nonmetro should return to 18.5."
assert round(fixed.loc["Metro", "rate_per_100k"], 1) == 14.1, "Metro should be 14.1."
assert fixed["population"].sum() < broken_summary["population"].sum(), \
    "The repaired denominator must be smaller — suppressed counties are out of it."
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Running is not checking
The broken version produced a clean table with plausible numbers and no warning. **Every
result in a report needs a reason to be believed that is stronger than the absence of an
error message.**
:::

# Exercise 7 — Visualise {.unnumbered background-color="#003594"}

## Exercise 7 — Visualise

**Worked example.** A two-bar comparison is the right figure for a two-group finding. The
zero baseline is what keeps the comparison honest, and the value labels remove the need to
read heights against a gridline.

```{pyodide}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.2))
bars = ax.bar(["Metro", "Nonmetro"],
              [summary.loc["Metro", "rate_per_100k"],
               summary.loc["Nonmetro", "rate_per_100k"]],
              color=["#003594", "#8a6400"], edgecolor="white")
ax.bar_label(bars, fmt="%.1f", padding=3)
ax.set_ylim(0, 22)
ax.set_ylabel("Firearm deaths per 100,000")
ax.set_title("Pooled 2023 firearm death rate, 42 reporting PA counties")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.figure-description}
**Figure 2.** Bar chart of the pooled 2023 firearm death rate for the 42 reporting
Pennsylvania counties. The metro bar, in royal blue, reaches 14.1 deaths per 100,000. The
nonmetro bar, in dark gold, reaches 18.5. Both bars are labelled with their value and the
vertical axis starts at zero.
:::

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex7_figure
#| hint: true
# The blank is the top of the axis — any number comfortably above 62, such
# as 80. The bottom is already 0, and that is the part that matters.
#
# Starting a bar axis anywhere above zero makes a small difference look
# enormous. Module 5 called this axis truncation; it is the commonest way
# an honest analyst draws a dishonest figure.
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex7_figure
#| solution: true
joined["suicides"] = joined["firearm_suicide"].fillna(0)
share = joined.groupby("metro").agg(deaths=("firearm_deaths", "sum"),
                                    suicides=("suicides", "sum"))
share["suicide_share_pct"] = share["suicides"] / share["deaths"] * 100

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.2))
bars = ax.bar(["Metro", "Nonmetro"],
              [share.loc["Metro", "suicide_share_pct"],
               share.loc["Nonmetro", "suicide_share_pct"]],
              color=["#003594", "#8a6400"], edgecolor="white")
ax.bar_label(bars, fmt="%.1f", padding=3)
ax.set_ylim(0, 80)
ax.set_ylabel("Suicide share of firearm deaths (%)")

plt.show()

print(share.round(1))
```

```{pyodide}
assert ax.get_ylim()[0] == 0, "A bar chart's axis starts at zero."
assert ax.get_ylim()[1] >= 62, "The axis must be tall enough to show the 62.1 bar."
assert ax.get_ylabel() != "", "Label the y-axis."
assert ax.get_title() != "", "Title the figure."
assert round(share.loc["Nonmetro", "suicide_share_pct"], 1) == 62.1, "Nonmetro share is 62.1%."
```

# Exercise 9 — Report the finding {.unnumbered background-color="#003594"}

## Exercise 9 — Report the finding

**Worked example.** A reported number is assembled from the pipeline's own variables rather
than typed by hand. A number typed by hand stops being a result the moment the data changes.

```{pyodide}
n_reporting = len(reporting)
nonmetro_rate = summary.loc["Nonmetro", "rate_per_100k"]

print(f"Among the {n_reporting} reporting counties, the nonmetro rate "
      f"was {nonmetro_rate:.1f} per 100,000.")
```

**Your turn.** Complete the finding sentence so that **both** rates come from `summary`, not
from your memory of the slide.

```{pyodide}

metro_rate = summary.loc["______", "rate_per_100k"]
nonmetro_deaths = int(summary.loc["Nonmetro", "deaths"])

finding = (
    f"Among the {n_reporting} Pennsylvania counties reporting a 2023 firearm death "
```

## Session outcomes {.smaller}

- The **seven-stage pipeline** — import, clean, join, group, summarise, visualise, report
- **Suppression** as a protective mechanism, and its non-random pattern
- **The silent denominator error**, and the fact that it reverses this finding
- **Notebook hygiene**: imports at the top, relative paths, seeds, restart-and-run-all
- **Uncertainty stated verbally** — counts, coverage, and consistency across years
- **The five-move report**, and computer output integrated into sentences

::: {.callout-tip}
## The finding, paid off
**Nonmetro 18.5 per 100,000 against metro 14.1**, with suicides at **62.1%** of nonmetro
firearm deaths against **54.7%** in metro counties. Handled carelessly, the same data reports
8.2 against 13.6 and confirms the opposite.
:::

**The final project applies this pipeline to a question of the student's own. The seven
stages do not change — only the question and the data do.**

::: {.notes}
Close by paying the promise off out loud, because it was made seventy-five minutes ago and
they earned it.

Everyone in this room believed, at the start, that firearm death is an urban problem.
Pennsylvania's data says eighteen point five against fourteen point one, the other direction,
and the suicide share tells you why. That is the only finding this course has shown them that
contradicts what they walked in with — every other one confirmed what a public health student
already suspects. Say that explicitly. It is why this one was saved for last.

And then the harder half, which is the real lesson. The wrong version of that analysis
produced eight point two against thirteen point six. Clean code, no errors, a table that looks
exactly as trustworthy as the right one — and it confirms the stereotype they arrived with.
That is the shape of the most dangerous kind of mistake: it runs, and it agrees with you.

For the project, the sentence to leave them with is that the pipeline does not change. New
question, new file, same seven stages. They have the whole skeleton now.
